svg.title: serial-broker at a glance
svg.desc: One page about serial-broker. First the problem: the Web Serial API lets one browsing context open a port, so a second tab is refused; with serial-broker one tab holds the port and every tab reads from it and writes to it. Then where the library sits: the tabs of one origin, each running the application and serial-broker, connected by a message bus made of a SharedWorker or a BroadcastChannel, on top of the browser's Web Locks, Web Serial and localStorage, and below them the serial devices. Then four situations: several tabs using one device, the tab holding the port closing or crashing, the device being unplugged, and a tab limit that gives one tab exclusive use. Finally what shows an operator what is happening — errors, logging, the diagnostics entry point and the debugging surface — and the calls an application makes.
svg.text: One serial port, every tab of an origin.
The Web Serial API gives one browsing context exclusive access to a port.

g.text: InvalidStateError – the port is already open
One tab opens the port, the others are refused.
That tab closes: no other tab takes over.
The device is unplugged: you write the recovery.
Every tab reads from and writes to the one port.
That tab closes: another tab takes over.
The device comes back: so does the connection.

svg.text: Everything runs in the browser, on your origin: no server component, no browser extension.

g.text: Browser · one origin · HTTPS or localhost
Message bus · a SharedWorker, or a BroadcastChannel where that is not available
the port, opened by the tab
which tab holds the port, and
the places a tab limit allows
One configuration per device, each with its own connection and its own recovery.
One file more for your web server: the worker script — and the debugging surface, if you serve it.
serial-broker is the transport only. Framing, checksums and request–response belong to your code above it.

svg.text: The situations a shared port runs into, and what the library does in each of them.

g.text: Several tabs need the same device
Every tab receives what the device sends and
can write to it; a write reaches it at most once.
The tab holding the port goes away
The browser frees its Web Lock however
the tab ends: no unload handler, no timeout.
The device is unplugged or switched off
Every tab sees the same status. The port
reopens with the same settings, on its own.
Only one tab may use the device
maxTabs: 1 gives one tab exclusive use.
The others wait, and take over when it ends.

svg.text: Which tab holds the port is invisible to the application on purpose — and visible to whoever operates it.

g.text: A stable code, the context it happened in, and one
sentence saying what to do about it.
Records to the logger you pass, each naming the tab
and configuration. Nothing is logged until you ask.
An observer on the bus: every tab, its role, status,
settings and pending writes. It takes no port.
The same state as a page, with the traffic and the
locks. Opening it never moves a port.

svg.text: The same calls in every tab
Chrome, Edge, Opera or Brave · HTTPS or localhost · all tabs on one origin · no runtime dependencies · MIT
